lead: The block diagram of a radar becomes real hardware here. The antenna must form a narrow beam and scan it; the transmitter must deliver short pulses of high power; the receiver must hear an echo near its own noise; and the duplexer must let one antenna serve both without burning the receiver. This chapter connects each block to the parts used in practice: dish and array antennas, magnetron, klystron and solid-state transmitters, superheterodyne receivers, displays, and TR-tube and circulator duplexers.
prereq: You need the block diagram from Radar principle, block diagram and frequency bands; microwave tubes and ferrite devices are covered in Microwave components, devices and measurements.

sections.h3: Antennas: dish, shaped beam and array

blocks.text: A radar antenna needs high gain and low sidelobes. A parabolic reflector with a feed at its focus forms a narrow pencil beam; its beamwidth is about 70λ/D degrees and its gain G = η(πD/λ)², where D is the diameter and η the aperture efficiency, about 0.55 to 0.7. Most search radars rotate the whole antenna in azimuth. Some move only the feed, for example a nodding feed for height finding on a rotating dish.

An air search radar often shapes its elevation beam as cosecant squared: the gain stays high near the horizon and falls as csc²θ above it, where θ is the elevation angle. Long-range targets near the horizon get full gain; close targets at high elevation get less, which they can afford. An aircraft flying at constant height then gives a nearly constant echo as it approaches.

A slotted-waveguide array, cut with rows of slots, is the flat antenna of most marine radars. A phased array uses many elements, each behind a phase shifter, and steers the beam by changing the phases, with no moving parts. A passive array shares one transmitter; an active array (AESA) has a transmit/receive module behind every element. A radome protects the antenna and must pass the radar band with little loss.

The magnetron is a crossed-field oscillator that gives high peak power cheaply, so marine and many weather radars use it. Its phase is random from pulse to pulse, so coherent processing needs special care. The klystron and the travelling-wave tube (TWT) are amplifiers that follow a stable low-power source, so they keep the phase coherence that MTI and pulse Doppler need. Solid-state transmitters combine many gallium nitride (GaN) or silicon modules; each gives modest peak power, so they use longer pulses with pulse compression.

Peak and average power are linked by the duty cycle: P<sub>av</sub> = P<sub>t</sub> × τ × PRF. The tube, the waveguide and the duplexer must survive P<sub>t</sub>; the cooling and the power supply are sized for P<sub>av</sub>.

The modulator switches the tube on for each pulse. A line-type modulator charges a pulse-forming network (PFN, a ladder of inductors and capacitors that acts as an artificial transmission line) and discharges it through a thyratron or solid-state switch into the tube through a pulse transformer; the pulse width is set by the network. A hard-tube (active-switch) modulator switches a stored high voltage on and off directly, so the pulse width can be changed. The rise time and the flat top shape the transmitted spectrum and its splatter into nearby channels.

The receiver is a superheterodyne. A low-noise amplifier (LNA) sets the noise figure. A mixer driven by the STALO (stable local oscillator) shifts the echo to the intermediate frequency (IF), often 30 or 60 MHz; an image filter before the mixer rejects the image band. The IF amplifier sets the bandwidth, about 1/τ, near the matched filter. Coherent radars then use I and Q phase detectors against the COHO to keep amplitude and phase; simple radars use a logarithmic amplifier, which squeezes the wide range from weak echoes to strong clutter into one display, and an envelope detector. A CFAR (constant false alarm rate) threshold then decides target or no target.

An A-scope plots echo amplitude against range for one direction. A B-scope plots range against azimuth on a rectangle. The PPI (plan position indicator) is a map: range outward from the centre, azimuth around it, with a sweep that rotates with the antenna. Modern displays are computer screens that show processed tracks over a map.

In a branch-type duplexer, the TR (transmit-receive) gas tube sits in the receiver branch and the ATR (anti-transmit-receive) tube in the transmitter branch. During the pulse both fire: the TR tube shorts the receiver branch, and a quarter-wave length of line turns that short into an open circuit at the junction, so the pulse goes to the antenna. Between pulses both are off: the unfired ATR tube, a quarter wave from the junction, blocks the transmitter branch, and the echo goes to the receiver. A balanced duplexer uses two hybrid couplers and two TR tubes and handles more power over a wider band. Modern sets use a ferrite circulator, with a limiter in front of the receiver.
The isolation the duplexer must give is set by the transmitter power and the power the receiver front end can survive:

I = 10 log10(Pt / Psafe)
Here I is the isolation in dB; Pt is the peak transmitter power in W; Psafe is the largest power the receiver can absorb in W.

At the start of each pulse, before the gas fully ionises, a short spike leaks through that is larger than the steady leakage, so a receiver protector (a diode limiter) clips it. After the pulse the TR tube takes a few microseconds to deionise; until it does, the receiver is deaf, and this recovery time adds to the minimum range c(τ + t<sub>rec</sub>)/2. The figure shows the power levels of the worked example.

examples.question: A radar transmitter gives 100 kW peak, and the receiver front end can safely absorb 10 mW. Find the duplexer isolation needed. A TR tube gives 60 to 70 dB: why is a receiver protector still fitted?
steps: P<sub>t</sub> = 100 × 10³ W = 10⁵ W; P<sub>safe</sub> = 10 × 10⁻³ W = 10⁻² W.
I = 10 log<sub>10</sub> 10⁷ = 70 dB. In dBm: +80 dBm must come down to +10 dBm.
A tube giving 60 to 70 dB meets this only at its best, and the spike at the start of the pulse leaks more than the steady value, so a diode limiter after the duplexer clips what gets through.
examples.answer: The duplexer must give 70 dB; because real tubes are only just good enough and the leading-edge spike is larger, a limiter protects the receiver.

examples.question: An S-band search radar at 3 GHz has a 4 m dish with efficiency 0.55, peak power 1 MW, pulse width 1 µs and PRF 1000 Hz. Find the beamwidth, the gain in dB and the average power.
examples.answer: θ ≈ 1.75°, G ≈ 8685 (39.4 dB) and P<sub>av</sub> = 1 kW: the waveguide carries 1 MW pulses while the cooling handles only 1 kW.

traps: Treating duplexer isolation as one number for all time. The leading-edge spike and the recovery period decide receiver damage and the minimum range.
Mixing up peak and average power. Average power is peak times duty cycle, and cooling follows the average.
Calling the magnetron an amplifier. It is an oscillator; the klystron and the TWT are amplifiers that keep phase coherence.
Saying a cosecant-squared beam gives up gain near the horizon. It keeps high gain near the horizon (far targets) and gives up gain at high elevation (near targets).
Thinking a radome is just a rain cover. A wet or badly designed radome lowers gain and raises sidelobes.

quiz.q: State the job of a duplexer in a radar.
quiz.a: It lets one antenna serve the transmitter and the receiver: the pulse goes to the antenna while the receiver is shielded, and between pulses the echo goes to the receiver.

quiz.q: Why does an air search radar use a cosecant-squared elevation pattern?
quiz.a: Gain falls as csc²θ above the horizon, so far targets near the horizon get full gain and near targets at high elevation get less. A target at constant height then gives a nearly constant echo as its range changes.

quiz.q: A radar has 50 kW peak power and the receiver safe limit is 5 mW. Find the required isolation.
Why is a klystron or TWT preferred to a magnetron in an MTI or pulse Doppler radar?
quiz.a: They are amplifiers that follow a stable source, so every pulse has a known phase. A magnetron is an oscillator that starts with a random phase on each pulse, which spoils pulse-to-pulse comparison unless the COHO is locked to each pulse.

quiz.q: A transmitter gives 80 kW peak with a duty cycle of 0.001. Find the average power.
A TR tube takes 1 µs to recover after a 0.5 µs pulse. Find the minimum range.
quiz.a: R<sub>min</sub> = c(τ + t<sub>rec</sub>)/2 = 3 × 10⁸ × 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 225 m. Closer echoes arrive while the receiver is still blocked.

quiz.q: What does a PPI display show?
quiz.a: A plan view: range as distance from the centre and azimuth as angle around it, with a sweep that turns with the antenna.

quiz.q: Why can a high steady isolation still allow receiver damage?
quiz.a: At the leading edge of each pulse the gas has not yet ionised, so a short spike leaks through that is larger than the steady leakage; a limiter is needed to clip it.

beyond: Radar front ends are moving to active arrays with a GaN transmit/receive module behind every element, and to digital beamforming, where each element is digitised and beams are formed in software. Single-chip radars at 60 and 77 GHz put the transmitter, receiver and processor on one die. Weather radars now transmit two polarisations to tell rain from hail. Search for "active phased array", "GaN T/R module" and "dual-polarisation weather radar" to go further.
